newsitem.title: INDIA: India "black money" estimated at $28 billion.
newsitem.headline: India "black money" estimated at $28 billion.

text.p: India's Planning Commission said on Monday that the country's undeclared "black money" fuelling a parallel economy has reached $28 billion.

"According to an estimate there was black money worth 400 billion rupees ($11.2 billion) in circulation in 1982," Planning Commission deputy chairman Madhu Dandavate told a seminar on poverty alleviation.
"But at present it has gone up to 1,000 billion rupees ($28 billion)," Dandavate, a socialist former finance minister, was quoted by the Press Trust of India as saying.
Dandavate effectively heads the commission that sets public spending priorities for the government. The commission is traditionally chaired by the prime minister.

Black money, or undeclared wealth, is generated primarily by tax evasion. Indian officials say black money stems from illegal trade practices including under invoicing of export bills and overinvoicing of imports.
Barely 14 million of a population of 950 million are taxpayers in India, which has a burgeoning middle class of around 300 million.

Finance Minister P. Chidambaram, seeking to boost revenue in a bold budget he presented for fiscal 1997/98 (April-March) last month, declared an amnesty for disclosures of black money until the end of the year.

Chidambaram said in his budget speech that people who disclosed their unaccounted-for wealth would be taxed at 30 percent, the highest proposed limit for personal tax in the new budget that will take effect from April 1.
The amnesty move has drawn praise and criticism from partners in Chidambaram's 15-party United Front coalition.
The Congress party, which supports the nine-month-old government reluctantly, has criticised the scheme, saying the tax rates for disclosures should be increased.
Chidambaram did not say how much revenue he expected to generate through the scheme.
Dandavate, regarded as the author of the scheme, said the government should plough back funds raised from the disclosures into social welfare schemes and basic education.
Dandavate said the rich should be taxed heavily because of their extremely visible expenditure on luxury items, PTI said.
"I am not confident whether the government will accept my suggestion to ruthlessly tax the creamy layer," he said. ($1=35.8 rupees)
